title: Start of Every Shuffled Copy
statement:
You get two lowercase strings, text and pattern. A substring of text is a shuffled copy of pattern if it has the same length and uses exactly the same letters the same number of times, in any order.

Return the start index of every shuffled copy in text, in increasing order. Copies may overlap. Return an empty list if there are none.

examples.why: "ab" at 0 and 3, and "ba" at 6, which is a shuffled copy too. "bc", "ca", "bx" and "xb" use other letters.
Copies can overlap: the windows at 0 and 1 share a letter.
The only window "aab" has the right set of letters but the wrong counts. Checking which letters appear, without counting them, would wrongly match it.

constraints: Both strings contain only lowercase English letters
hints: Two strings are shuffled copies of each other exactly when their letter counts match. How much does the count change when a fixed-length window slides by one?
Keep a count of the letters in the current window of length pattern.length. Sliding right adds one letter and removes one; that is two updates, not a full recount.
Track how many of the 26 letters currently have matching counts. Each slide changes at most two letters, so you can update that number in O(1) and record the start whenever it is 26.

explain.intuition:
Order does not matter, only counts. So describe the pattern by its 26 letter counts and every window of the same length by its counts too. A window is a match exactly when the two count arrays are equal.

All windows have the same length, so sliding from one to the next just adds the entering letter and removes the leaving one. Instead of comparing all 26 counts each time, keep a number matches: how many letters currently have equal counts in the window and the pattern. Each slide touches two letters, and for each one you can see whether it just became equal or just stopped being equal.
steps: If the pattern is longer than the text, return an empty list.
Count the pattern's letters into need and the first window's letters into have. Set matches to the number of letters where they agree.
For each next start i: add the entering letter text[i + m − 1] and remove the leaving letter text[i − 1]. For each, before and after the change, adjust matches if that letter's equality flipped.
pitfalls: Comparing which letters appear instead of how often, as in the third example.
Re-sorting or recounting each window, which is O(n · m) and too slow for long patterns.
Recording the window's end index instead of its start.

solutions.title: Sort every window
solutions.idea: Sort the pattern once, then sort each window of the same length and compare.

solutions.title: Sliding counts with a match counter
solutions.idea: Keep the window's letter counts and how many of the 26 letters agree with the pattern. Each slide updates two letters.

followups: The alphabet is all of Unicode instead of 26 letters. How do you keep the per-slide work O(1)?
Return the longest substring that is a shuffled copy of some substring of the pattern.
